discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking methods (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber mirror) that created the solid-state femtosecond laser

nominees.name: Peter F. Moulton
nominees.affiliation: MIT Lincoln Laboratory (retired) / Q-Peak Inc., USA

motivation: Almost all of ultrafast science rests on one robust laser platform. Moulton invented the titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982), whose very broad gain bandwidth can support pulses of a few femtoseconds. Sibbett and co-workers found self-mode-locking in Ti:sapphire (1991), now explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, which produced clean femtosecond pulses with no dyes. Keller invented the semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM, 1992), which made passive mode-locking reliable and self-starting across solid-state, fibre and semiconductor lasers. Together these replaced fragile dye lasers with practical sources. They seed chirped pulse amplifiers, generate optical frequency combs and attosecond pulses, and are used in multiphoton microscopy, eye surgery and precision machining. Recent Nobel Prizes for chirped pulse amplification, frequency combs and attosecond physics all relied on these oscillators. The enabling invention itself has not yet been recognised.
